newsitem.title: USA: Clint Eastwood takes stand in civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Clint Eastwood takes stand in civil trial.

text.p: Clint Eastwood said on Monday he signed a secret deal with Warner Bros. to protect the studio from any potential losses from films directed by his ex-lover, Sondra Locke, who is suing him.
Locke, who met Eastwood on the set of the 1975 movie "The Outlaw Josey Wales," alleges in her suit that Eastwood essentially destroyed her directorial career in Hollywood.
Eastwood, speaking in curt, one-word sentences, testified at a civil trial that Locke had no knowledge of the deal, which she alleges helped sabotoge her career as a director and actress.

Eastwood, known for playing Hollywood tough men of few words, answered just "yes", "no" or "that's right" to about a dozen questions from Locke's lawyer, who rested her case after five minutes. Eastwood's lawyer said he would cross-examine the star later, probably on Tuesday.
The case stems from Locke's original 1989 palimony lawsuit against the Oscar-winning director and actor Eastwood in which she claimed assets the couple accumulated during their relationship.

Locke later dropped the palimony suit when Eastwood agreed to secure the director's contract worth $1.5 million at Warner Bros. for her. But Locke now claims that contract was "a sham" and is seeking damages of over $2.5 million.
Last week Locke testified that when she found out about the deal, "I felt annoyed, I felt embarrassed, I felt humiliated."
After the hearing adjourned for the day, Locke spoke to reporters outside the courthouse.

"If it weren't so serious, it might be funny in there," she said of the scene in court, where she and the man she lived with for 13 years sat at opposite ends of a table, separated by lawyers and avoiding eye contact.

During questioning by Locke's lawyer Peggy Garrity, Eastwood admitted he had signed an indemnity contract with Warner Bros. Pictures agreeing to pay almost $1.5 million to cover the studio for losses it might incur from a contract it had with Locke to direct.

Her directorial efforts, "Ratboy" in 1986 and "Impulse" in 1989, were not commercial successes and in three years under the Warner Bros. contract, none of her 30 suggested projects was ever developed into a film.
Eastwood's lawyer, Raymond Fisher, contends the actor-director had no intent to defraud Locke and only made the deal with Warner Bros. to help her directorial career.

In earlier testimony on Monday, Locke's personal manager Erik Magrath told the six-man, six-woman jury that since "Impulse", for which she was paid $350,000, she had only made one independent movie, "Do Me a Favour", for $10,000 this year.

"It goes to the truism that you're only as good as your last picture," Magrath said, adding that it was difficult for Locke to get any work now in Hollywood. "They've all passed on Sondra," he told Garrity.

Another witness, Albert Ruddy, who was a producer of the Oscar-winning film, "The Godfather", said he had known both Locke and Eastwood for at least 12 years. He testified it was not unusual for movie ideas not to pan out.
"I have been in many development deals that did not become (movies)," he said.
And Warner Bros. movie executive Bill Gerber, when asked by Fisher if it was unusual for films not to be made, replied "no."
